Berobenatide: Pfizer's Once-Monthly Injectable GLP-1 Peptide Enters Phase 3 — Research Dossier

Medical Disclaimer: Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use where applicable. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

What Is Berobenatide?

Berobenatide (development code PF'3944, formerly designated a Metsera compound) is an investigational long-acting peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) being developed by Pfizer for the treatment of chronic obesity and overweight with weight-related comorbidities. Its defining characteristic is an extended half-life engineered to support once-monthly subcutaneous dosing — a frequency no currently approved GLP-1-class drug achieves. If its Phase 3 program succeeds and FDA approval is obtained, berobenatide would be the first monthly injectable GLP-1 RA for obesity, reducing injection burden from 52 injections per year (weekly dosing) to just 12.

Berobenatide was developed by Metsera, a metabolic biotechnology company, before Pfizer acquired Metsera in a multi-billion-dollar transaction. The acquisition brought berobenatide and a companion ultra-long-acting amylin analog (PF'3945) into Pfizer's pipeline, positioning the company as a late entrant in the high-growth GLP-1 obesity market with a differentiated monthly dosing strategy.

Mechanism of Action

Berobenatide is a selective agonist of the GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R), targeting the same receptor as semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) and liraglutide (Victoza/Saxenda). GLP-1R agonism drives:

  • Appetite suppression: GLP-1R activation in the hypothalamus and brainstem (arcuate nucleus, NTS, area postrema) reduces hunger and increases satiety signals, leading to reduced caloric intake
  • Gastric emptying delay: Slower stomach emptying extends satiety after meals and blunts postprandial glucose spikes
  • Glucose-dependent insulin secretion: Enhances pancreatic beta cell insulin release only when blood glucose is elevated (glucose-dependent mechanism reduces hypoglycemia risk)
  • Glucagon suppression: Reduces postprandial glucagon, contributing to improved glucose control

The extended half-life enabling monthly dosing is achieved via proprietary peptide backbone modification and fatty acid conjugation technology designed to substantially extend the in vivo half-life beyond the approximately 7 days achieved by semaglutide. The specific extension chemistry has not been fully disclosed by Pfizer.

Key Research Findings

VESPER-1 (Weekly Dosing — 32-Week Extension)

VESPER-1 established berobenatide's efficacy backbone at weekly dosing. Full extension data presented at ADA 2026 (June 6, 2026):

  • Weight loss: 15.9% mean body weight reduction from baseline at 32 weeks (8 months) with the highest weekly dose in adults with obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes
  • Efficacy continues through 32 weeks with no sign of plateau
  • Tolerability consistent with the GLP-1 class (predominantly mild-moderate GI adverse events)

VESPER-3 (Monthly Dosing — Pivotal Phase 2b)

The differentiation trial for berobenatide. VESPER-3 tested once-monthly subcutaneous dosing. Results (ADA 2026):

  • Weight loss: Up to 12.3% placebo-adjusted mean weight loss at week 28 with the 4.8 mg monthly dose
  • Dose-dependent weight loss across monthly dose arms
  • Tolerability: Favorable profile described by Pfizer; predominantly mild-moderate GI events
  • 12.3% placebo-adjusted weight loss at 28 weeks is a clinically meaningful monthly dosing result, comparable to or exceeding the best-in-class monthly injectable GLP-1 RA benchmarks

Combination Program (SOLIS-1)

Pfizer is also studying berobenatide in combination with an ultra-long-acting amylin analog (PF'3945/MET-233i) in the Phase 2b SOLIS-1 trial. This combination strategy follows the dual-mechanism approach validated by CagriSema (cagrilintide + semaglutide) and EloraTZP (eloralintide + tirzepatide), where amylin and GLP-1 receptor pathways operate synergistically through distinct neural circuits. No results from SOLIS-1 are available as of November 2026.

Phase 3 Program (VESPER-6 and beyond)

Pfizer announced a Phase 3 program comprising 10 trials for berobenatide in 2026:

  • VESPER-6: Pivotal Phase 3 efficacy and safety trial; enrollment opened 2026. This is the registration study required for FDA NDA submission for the obesity indication.
  • Additional trials cover type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular outcomes, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease — the full portfolio of comorbidity benefit studies required for label differentiation in the competitive obesity market.
  • A pivotal 9.6 mg high monthly dose arm is planned for Phase 3.

Dosing in Research

Phase 2b dosing: 4.8 mg once monthly (VESPER-3, most efficacious dose reported). Phase 3 plans include a 9.6 mg monthly arm. Weekly doses were also tested in VESPER-1 (specific mg not fully disclosed in public summaries). All doses are subcutaneous injection. Berobenatide is not available outside of clinical trials. Dosing information is provided for educational purposes only.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is berobenatide different from weekly semaglutide or tirzepatide?

Berobenatide is a selective GLP-1R agonist (like semaglutide), not a dual GLP-1/GIP agonist (like tirzepatide). Its primary differentiator is dosing convenience: once-monthly injection vs. once-weekly for competitors. VESPER-3 monthly Phase 2b showed 12.3% placebo-adjusted weight loss at 28 weeks — clinically meaningful at a monthly dosing interval that reduces annual injections from 52 to 12. No head-to-head data vs. weekly agents have been published.

What weight loss did berobenatide achieve in the VESPER-3 trial?

VESPER-3 reported up to 12.3% placebo-adjusted mean weight loss at week 28 with the 4.8 mg once-monthly dose (ADA 2026, June 2026). The weekly dosing VESPER-1 extension achieved 15.9% at 32 weeks, which is higher but requires weekly rather than monthly injections. Phase 3 will test a 9.6 mg monthly dose that may achieve higher efficacy than the 4.8 mg Phase 2b arm.

What is the Pfizer and Metsera connection for berobenatide?

Berobenatide originated at Metsera, a metabolic disease biotech. Pfizer acquired Metsera for approximately $7–10 billion, gaining berobenatide and the companion amylin analog PF'3945 as lead assets. Pfizer has committed to a 10-trial Phase 3 program, with the pivotal VESPER-6 enrolling in 2026 — a scale comparable to Novo Nordisk's and Lilly's obesity programs. The acquisition was Pfizer's primary strategic entry into the GLP-1 obesity market.

Research Limitations

  • No Phase 3 efficacy results available as of November 2026; VESPER-6 and other Phase 3 trials are ongoing or not yet completed.
  • No head-to-head trial against weekly semaglutide or tirzepatide.
  • Extension chemistry and peptide sequence not fully publicly disclosed.
  • Long-term cardiovascular outcome data not available; cardiovascular outcomes trial planned.
  • Phase 2b efficacy (12.3% at 28 weeks, monthly) is based on single Phase 2b study; Phase 3 may show different results.
  • SOLIS-1 combination trial (berobenatide + PF'3945) has no published results.

Disclaimer

Berobenatide is an investigational compound not approved by the FDA or any regulatory authority worldwide for any indication as of November 2026. This dossier is intended for educational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. Do not attempt to obtain or use this compound outside of an authorized clinical trial. Consult a licensed healthcare provider for any weight management or metabolic health concerns.
